OPA/Toxiproxy and a live three-role LLM workflow with networked MCP tools reproduce the persisted-but-not-enforced boundary on narrower surfaces. Finally, an unmodified external MCPMark agent executes 60 closed-loop task arms. Normal C4 denies all 31 exposed post-barrier calls and commits no effect; selective C3 allows 344 calls and commits 145 effects across Filesystem and PostgreSQL. Transport success is therefore evidence of progress, not a revocation-completion verdict.
entries.title: Revocation Is Not Complete at Receipt: An Executable Outcome Contract for Distributed Agent-Tool Gateways

entries.abstract: Authorization checks at individual tool calls do not reveal how long earlier authority remains usable. We study this lifecycle failure as privilege creep: a capability stays reachable after its last justified workflow step. We present CreepScope, a trace-oriented evaluation protocol that samples reachable authority at every step and separates no-remaining-use exposure into stale-after-use and never-required components; Capability-Step Exposure (CSE) counts total stepwise overexposure and Residual Privilege Debt (RPD) the terminal residue, while stale-after-use exposure is the direct privilege-creep measure. A 96-cell deterministic replay over 12 controlled storage, communication, and cloud-operation workflows validates these semantics: Static Task Scope and Monotonic On-Demand retain mean CSEs of 26 and 13, whereas an oracle-controlled Step Lease has zero CSE and zero residual debt by construction. All three persistent regimes share the same stale-after-use exposure of 13, so their CSE differences come from scope and grant timing rather than post-use retention; Full Access alone adds 91.33 never-required capability-steps. A separate 24-episode local case then lets Qwen2 7B choose tools in one simulated mail workflow: the injected stale send executes in all nine persistent-policy episodes and in none of the three Step-Lease episodes, while all 24 required action sequences complete. These results establish a reproducible containment case, not cross-workflow or cross-model effectiveness. Core metrics are reconstructed from raw events, and exact gates reject incomplete or duplicated evaluation grids.
entries.title: CreepScope: Measuring Post-Use Authorization Exposure in Tool-Using Agents

entries.abstract: This paper investigates a new role of randomness in stochastic policies--as a medium for embedding and communicating information. Specifically, we consider an agent interacting with an environment according to a prescribed stochastic policy. By carefully modulating the random action realizations of the policy, information can be embedded into the agent's behavior without altering the prescribed action distribution. We cast this problem as a channel coding problem, in which the controlled system implicitly serves as a communication channel. We then propose a coding scheme, termed posterior-matching randomness modulation (PRAM), that selects actions according to the message to be transmitted. With the aid of common randomness independent of the control system, PRAM preserves the prescribed action distribution for every state and every message. We further prove that PRAM is asymptotically reliable: the message can be decoded with arbitrarily small error probability as the observed state trajectory becomes sufficiently long. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in applications including multi-bit policy watermarking and trajectory provenance.
entries.title: Embedding Information in Policy Randomness: Distribution-Preserving Implicit Communication in MDPs

entries.abstract: AI agents built on different language models can still share the software that presents their choices. We study one shared component, the order in which a borrowing agent's actions are listed, in a simulated collateralized lending market populated by three open-weight model families. In fixed decision states, moving the borrowing action from last to first raises valid borrowing requests by 27 percentage points. In 12 matched pairs of 15-agent markets, all agents in one market see the same order; the other spreads the six possible orders across agents. A common order moves whole markets: the four markets that listed borrowing first raised net debt by 1.8 to 2.7 times their initial unused borrowing capacity, while those that listed debt reduction first cut debt. These groups account for 96 percent of the sample variation among common markets, whose standard deviation is three times the balanced one. The borrowing cap stops 40 percent of valid borrowing requests made when borrowing is listed first, but it values collateral at the pool price, so correlated purchases raise borrowing capacity and leave positions above 70 percent of reference value. Under a 30 percent shock, an 8 percent liquidation bonus produces write-offs on loans that are fully collateralized before liquidation, and liquidation triggers that read the pool price add exposure. Common ordering does not put more borrowers into the write-off zone; it concentrates them in the markets whose shared order favored borrowing. Collateral valuation and liquidation rules determine how much of it creditors fail to recover.
entries.title: Requested, Executed and Recoverable Credit: Shared Action Ordering among LLM Borrowers in a Simulated Lending Market

entries.abstract: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, exposing a cooperator to partners with diverse strategies during training is key to better collaboration at test time. However, existing methods typically rely on trajectory-level proxies to measure diversity, which may label two distinct trajectories of the same strategy as diverse. Instead, our key insight is to leverage LLMs' ability to describe behaviorally distinct agents in environments, similar to how humans can recognize high-level strategies. To this end, we introduce PopGen, a framework that synthesizes semantically diverse agents from scratch using LLMs. PopGen first generates a diverse set of textual descriptions of agent behaviors, then translates each behavior into a code policy that can be executed within the environment. We show that cooperators trained against PopGen populations achieve robust zero-shot cooperation with unseen partners, outperforming population-play baselines across four collaborative environments. We further show that semantic diversity scales with PopGen population size, improving the cooperator's worst-case performance, and we identify design choices that preserve population quality while maximizing diversity. Our code is available at https://github.com/labicon/PopGen.
entries.title: PopGen: Generating Semantically Diverse Populations for Zero-Shot Coordination

entries.abstract: We present a low-cost miniature Ackermann vehicle for embedded neural-driving research, organized as a hardware-partitioned perceive-decide-act agent: an ESP32 camera node streams frames over Wi-Fi to a host computer, where neural inference and state estimation run, while an ESP32-S3 chassis controller executes safety-critical actuation in a 100 Hz per-wheel proportional-integral-derivative (PID) loop beneath a micro-ROS client. The partition isolates real-time control and safety on the vehicle while learning-based components run off-board, supervised by an operator from a gamepad. We characterize the complete pipeline during real closed-loop neural driving. Wireless sensing, rather than neural inference, dominates latency, with a 59.5 ms median capture-to-actuation delay; the platform absorbed wireless variability by holding the last safe command under a firmware watchdog, operating across twelve autonomous sessions with zero collisions or manual interventions; and encoder-inertial-measurement-unit (IMU) fusion cut odometry loop-closure error by 22%. These results indicate that carefully partitioned microcontroller-class vehicles support reproducible experiments in embedded AI, wireless control, and operator-supervised autonomous driving. The platform software is open source.
entries.title: A Hardware-Partitioned micro-ROS Mini-Vehicle for Operator-Supervised Neural Driving

entries.abstract: A self-evolving agent rewrites its own harness and must decide which rewrites to keep, so its improvement signal is the check a rewrite has to pass. Verifying a rewrite by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, while executable checks such as the repository's own tests are too sparse to catch behavior-changing rewrites, rejecting only a quarter of them. We instead take test feedback as the executable signal, and search for test suites that are both small and strong with a quality-diversity evolutionary algorithm, so that the signal is dense and informative. TeSearch treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so that quality is pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on that descriptor. Across 129 real-world modules and three backbones, TeSearch delivers the highest-quality suites of any method compared, LLM-driven evolutionary search included, and the smallest of any LLM-based one. Used as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent, it rejects 59.9% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3% for the repository's tests, at a 4.0% false-alarm rate and 3.5 s per decision. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/TeSearch.
entries.comment: In NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Self-Evolving Diversity-Driven Search for Robust AI Systems (EvoRobust)
entries.title: Small but Mighty: Test Suites as Improvement Signals for Self-Evolving Agents

entries.abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning a language model to a narrow task makes it misaligned on unrelated ones. Because organizations now routinely fine-tune models on their own data, it matters which kinds of training data cause EM. So far, studies have induced EM with data containing recognized safety failures, such as insecure code or harmful advice, while biased training data is typically examined by fairness research for the bias models learn from it rather than for its effects on safety. In real-world text, much of this bias, such as demographic stereotypes, appears not as derogatory language but politely, embedded in judgments about people. We ask whether learning such polite stereotypes can itself cause EM. We find that fine-tuning on polite answers that rely on stereotypes makes models less safe and less truthful on unrelated tasks. The effect holds across four open-weight model families (7B to 12B), both gender and race stereotypes, and repeated training runs, relative to controls trained on the same questions without the stereotype. We further show that the learned stereotype has its own direction in model activations, distinct from directions for generic misaligned traits such as deception. This direction exists before fine-tuning and can both control the learned stereotype and monitor its acquisition. Existing defenses against EM improve safety while leaving the stereotype largely intact. Beyond this controlled setting, fine-tuning on political news coverage also triggers EM, apparently amplified by partisan framing, and stereotype models acting as tool-using agents can carry out harmful tasks and blame people without evidence. Our results show that biased training data is not only a fairness problem but also a safety one. We argue that EM is studied too narrowly, and that fairness concerns and methods offer a natural way to broaden the search for its triggers.
entries.title: Unfair and Unsafe: Everyday Bias Triggers Emergent Misalignment

entries.abstract: Satellite mega-constellations are emerging as large-scale sensing, communication, and computation fabrics, yet their learning architectures remain largely inherited from terrestrial federated learning and ground-centric mission operations--- ill-suited to satellites that differ by orders of magnitude in Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWAP-C), radiation tolerance, link availability, and propagation delay. We propose a heterogeneous federated learning method based on the FractalNet architecture for orbital edge intelligence. We formalize contact-window-constrained, depth-heterogeneous federated optimization and introduce a distributed path scheduler that assigns model depth as a function of SWAP-C constraints, predicted inter-satellite contacts, and training statistics. To reduce message overhead and energy consumption, each tier pools updates periodically rather than at every contact opportunity, and a three-tier agentic control plane governs in-space scheduling, anomaly escalation, and policy-governed autonomy. As a case study, we apply the framework to wildfire detection, where each orbital shell naturally learns a different semantic level of situational awareness: pixel-scale thermal anomalies at low Earth orbit (LEO), regional fire-front dynamics at medium Earth orbit (MEO), and larger-scale risk propagation at geostationary or high Earth orbit (GEO/HEO). Experiments on simulated mega-constellations validate the approach across convergence, communication efficiency, energy adaptation, scheduled-pooling savings, robustness, and latency.
entries.title: FractalNet-Based Heterogeneous Federated Learning for Orbital Edge Intelligence in Satellite Mega-Constellations: A Wildfire Case Study

entries.abstract: Agent skills occupy a privileged position in the agent workflow, as agents are expected to implicitly follow and execute them, rendering third-party skills a vulnerable attack surface. Existing studies have revealed unsafe agent behaviors induced by skill-based attacks, but they primarily evaluate poisoned skills within a single task execution and enumerate harms through ad hoc risk lists. To bridge these gaps, we introduce SkillHarm, a benchmark of skill-based attacks across the skill-use lifecycle, paired with a systematic taxonomy of skill-relevant risks. SkillHarm evaluates two attack scenarios: Fixed-Payload Poisoning (FPP), where a fixed poisoned skill package directly compromises any task session that invokes it, and Self-Mutating Poisoning (SMP), where an initially benign execution silently mutates persistent skill content, deferring harm until a subsequent reuse. It further defines 12 risk types based on the agent workflow component targeted by the harm: data pipelines, system environments, and agent autonomy. To instantiate these attacks at scale, we build AutoSkillHarm, an automated construction pipeline with coding agents driven by natural-language harnesses. The resulting benchmark contains 879 attack samples across 71 skills. Experiments show that current agents remain vulnerable with attack success rates up to 86.3% in FPP and 69.3% in SMP. Our analysis further reveals a latent risk: many apparent attack failures stem from the agent failing to engage with the poisoned file rather than genuine resistance, and current defenses still fail to reliably mitigate the threat.
entries.title: SkillHarm: Lifecycle-Aware Skill-Based Attacks via Automated Construction

entries.abstract: With the rapid increase in interest towards large scale earth observing satellite constellations, the problem of properly commanding and utilizing these systems has become increasingly relevant. This work focuses on a complete distributed approach to this problem, incorporating an observation task allocation and scheduling algorithm in addition to a sensor data fusion algorithm for end-to-end target coverage and processing. Observation task allocation and scheduling is performed in this work through the combination of the bid warped consensus based bundle algorithm (BWCBBA) and a lightweight observation scheduler for bid scoring. This method produces a unique mapping of tasks to command agents when allowed to iterate sufficiently. The approach to distributed data fusion in this work occurs primarily through an ownership model in which one satellite takes ownership of a system track in the constellation. After local information is shared between the sensing nodes to create the system tracks, the dedicated fusion nodes assume ownership for further information fusion and track information is disseminated throughout the constellation for data association. This paper analyzes the performance of these two algorithms over a set of increasingly decentralized architectures to highlight the performance losses compared to more traditional centralized methods.
entries.comment: Presented at the 2026 AAS Rocky Mountain GN&C Conference, Breckenridge, CO (AAS 26-027). 19 pages, 16 figures
entries.title: Distributed Observation Scheduling and Sensor Fusion For Large Agile Constellations

entries.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) engage tools, share memory, and delegate tasks, often encountering adversarial content. Current defenses for MAS are typically evaluated in isolation, focusing on one attack type at a time, which can lead to costly and hard-to-audit outcomes. This study organizes defenses into five principles, implementing them as DEFER1 (DEterministic-First Enforcement with Residual judgment), which includes a cascade of 28 checks that blocks what it can and refers the rest to a panel of four judges. In independent testing across four domains, attack success rates drop from about 30.0% to approximately 3.0%, with 78% of blocked attacks handled by deterministic checks. Only a quarter of proposals reach the judges in the security-operations domain, illustrating that the rules provide security for attacks violating clear policies, while judges manage those that only misrepresent intent. Both systems have weaknesses, such as a risk-score approval gate that inaccurately approves most attack proposals but few legitimate ones, highlighting the challenges in assessing threats accurately.
entries.title: Where Rules End and Judges Begin: Measuring the Judgment Boundary in Multi-Agent Systems Security

entries.abstract: Recent trackers built on foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) achieve strong performance by propagating object masks through memory. However, this strength is also a key source of failure: under occlusion, reappearance, or distractors, an incorrect prediction can enter the tracking loop and be propagated over time, resulting in persistent identity drift. Existing approaches seek to prevent such failures through improved memory and temporal modeling, but once a failure occurs, the tracker has no explicit mechanism to recognize or correct it. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. A vision-language verification agent first reasons over spatio-temporal context to determine whether the tracker is still following the target. When a failure is detected, a correction agent uses temporal context to recover the target before tracking continues. The correction agent is trained on real SAM3 failures, augmented with targeted identity-switch and distractor perturbations that expose it to challenging ambiguities during recovery. On LVOS-v2 and SecVOS, Dual-Agent improves SAM3 by 1.2 and 2.7 $J\&F$, respectively. Importantly, the proposed framework transfers without retraining to SAM2.1, SeC, and Cutie, as well as to long-term video object tracking benchmarks including LaSOT-ext, TNL2K, and VOT-LT2022. Our results show that explicitly reasoning about when tracking fails and how to recover provides a complementary path to robust tracking beyond improving propagation alone. Project page: valaybundele.github.io/Dual-Agent.
entries.title: When Trackers Fail: VLM-Guided Verification and Recovery for Robust Video Object Segmentation

entries.abstract: Agent environments are essential for large language model (LLM) development. They use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards. Verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training. As agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers. To this end, we ask whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking. We introduce a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening. It first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities. We apply this loop to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments. The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of our hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments. Project page: https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.
entries.title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments

entries.abstract: With ever increasing personalized large language model (LLM) services, the next question to answer is how to improve the quality of services/users' experiences, which is indicated by personalized LLM generation accuracy/quality and inference latency. Although state-of-the-art designs, e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or Full PEFT+RAG, can help, they largely ignore the heterogeneous semantic concentrations of users' historical data and cannot fully unleash the potential of personal data for personalized LLM performance enhancement. In this paper, we propose PEFT Union RAG (PUR), a novel ``fast and accurate'' approach that exploits the semantic concentration of users' personal historical data to split workload between PEFT and RAG, aiming to improve personalized LLM performance in terms of better generation accuracy/quality and lower inference latency. Briefly, PUR partitions user's personal historical data and assigns semantic concentrated ``core'' information to PEFT for offline parametric fine-tuning, while retaining dispersed information for RAG. During the online LLM inference, PUR directly generates responses for ``core'' queries covered by the PEFT region and invokes RAG only for sporadic ``peripheral'' queries. Experimental results show that, by appropriately splitting workload between PEFT and RAG, PUR consistently achieves the best generation accuracy/quality for various users across multiple tasks, while reducing inference latency by 14.4%--46.6% compared with the best performed method.
entries.title: Fast and Accurate: Improving Personalized LLM Performance by Semantic Concentration Inspired Workload Split between RAG and Fine-Tuning

entries.abstract: Reusable skills improve multimodal agents without updating model weights, but their effectiveness depends on both the evidence presented and the procedure used to read it. We introduce ViewCraft, which jointly evolves an executable evidence interface and its reading procedure. The interface selects, transforms, and organizes observations; the reader interprets the resulting views. Failure traces guide revisions, replay and paired evaluation retain useful changes, and interface projection recovers visual edits from eligible rejected joint proposals. Across eight benchmarks, ViewCraft improves over direct execution by an average of $6.1$ points in task score, with gains on every benchmark. The advantage persists at a matched input-token budget. On all five multi-source tasks, the learned interface uses 8%-15% fewer input tokens than Initial skill. The learned skills also transfer across executors and outperform direct execution in every evaluated transfer, supporting evidence construction and reading as a coupled, reusable skill.
entries.title: VIEWCRAFT: Evolving What Multimodal Agents See and How They Read It

entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in clinical decision support. However, existing approaches often rely on multi-step reasoning or multi-agent collaboration to execute clinical guidelines, introducing substantial computational overhead without reliably preventing decision errors. To address these limitations, we propose a framework for Medical Decision Execution (MedDEx) that integrates structured patient states with deterministic rule execution to support guideline-based treatment planning. MedDEx separates clinical record interpretation from guideline execution, leveraging LLMs to extract patient information and generate treatment plans while assigning guideline-defined decision logic to a rule executor. Experiments across multiple clinical guideline benchmarks demonstrate that MedDEx improves decision accuracy while reducing inference costs. Further analyses highlight the critical roles of structured patient representations and deterministic rule execution, suggesting that additional LLM reasoning does not necessarily translate into better guideline adherence.
entries.title: More Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Executing Clinical Guidelines with LLMs and Rules

entries.abstract: Cellular reprogramming, the artificial transformation of one cell type into another, has been attracting increasing research attention due to its therapeutic potential for complex diseases. However, identifying effective reprogramming strategies through classical wet-lab experiments is hindered by lengthy time commitments and high costs. In this study, we explore the use of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to control Boolean network models of complex biological systems, such as gene regulatory and signalling pathway networks. We formulate a novel control problem for Boolean network models under the asynchronous update mode, specifically in the context of cellular reprogramming. To solve it, we devise GATTACA, a scalable computational framework. To facilitate scalability of our framework, we consider previously introduced concept of a pseudo-attractor and improve the procedure for effective identification of pseudo-attractor states. We then incorporate graph neural networks with graph convolution operations into the artificial neural network approximator of the DRL agent's action-value function. This allows us to leverage the available knowledge on the structure of a biological system and to indirectly, yet effectively, encode the system's modelled dynamics into a latent representation. Experiments on several large-scale, real-world biological networks from the literature demonstrate the scalability and effectiveness of our approach.
entries.title: Graph Neural Network-Based Reinforcement Learning for Controlling Biological Networks - the GATTACA Framework

entries.abstract: Deep Research agents rely on long-horizon reasoning and iterative tool use to solve complex information-seeking tasks. However, adaptive decision-making over these trajectories remains challenging, as agents may stop prematurely when further evidence is needed, continue unnecessarily after sufficient evidence has been gathered, or fail to redirect unproductive trajectories. Existing solutions either require costly model retraining and dense turn-level supervision, or rely on heuristic control rules that are not directly optimized for downstream research utility. This motivates a lightweight, utility-aware alternative for Deep Research control. We formulate adaptive rerouting in long-horizon Deep Research as a state-conditioned trajectory correction problem. Based on this view, we introduce RIVO, a lightweight plug-in framework for adaptive trajectory correction. The agent estimates its research state from lightweight signals and determines whether trajectory redirection is needed. Once triggered, the plug-in modifies the Host token logits to steer generation toward a more promising research direction. Theoretical analysis shows that, under a value-alignment condition and bounded local curvature, a sufficiently small logit intervention can locally improve expected downstream research utility. We further construct BrowseCore, a curated dataset with a paired local corpus, for efficient and controlled Deep Research experimentation. Building on this resource, the plug-in is trained from downstream outcomes, enabling it to learn corrections that improve subsequent research and final task performance. Extensive experiments across multiple Deep Research benchmarks and control settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, showing that lightweight logit intervention can improve long-horizon research without retraining the underlying Host model.
entries.title: RIVO: Lightweight Adaptive Rerouting for Deep Research Agents

entries.abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) have shown strong capability in solving complex tasks by assigning different agents specialized roles and corresponding subtasks. However, agents may overstep their assigned responsibilities and perform subtasks belonging to other roles, which can disrupt workflow, reduce system efficiency, and degrade task performance. To address this issue, we investigate role-related patterns in the model's internal activation space and uncover two key observations: (i) role instructions induce consistent directional shifts in activation space, and (ii) role-adherent and role-overstepping trajectories exhibit distinct activation patterns. Based on these observations, we propose Dynamic Role Activation Steering (DRAS), a lightweight and effective inference-time activation intervention approach to reduce role overstepping in multi-agent collaboration. Specifically, DRAS constructs a role steering vector and a lightweight role-overstepping detector for each role. During LLM generation, the detector estimates the probability of role overstepping from the current activation state, and DRAS dynamically adjusts the steering strength accordingly to guide the agent toward its assigned responsibilities. Experimental results show that DRAS effectively reduces the number of role-overstepping trajectories by up to 86.6% compared with Vanilla MAS, thereby improving task quality score by 10.0%--11.1%, achieving a 1.50$\times$--1.61$\times$ task-completion speedup, and reducing token consumption by 26.8%--38.7%.
entries.title: Mind Your Own Role: Reducing Role Overstepping for Effective and Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Dynamic Role Activation Steering

entries.abstract: Quantum decoherence does not permit the operation of (new) miniaturised devices or protocols that can otherwise run unassisted in classical settings, without explicit user agent intervention in the quantum realm. Classical driving signals are inadequate to model a truly quantum device built entirely in the quantum realm. Synchronisation endures miniaturisation without sacrificing quantum coherence, unlike thermalisation. We quantise the Kuramoto model and the Van der Pol oscillator and couple it with qubit(s) to show a robust limit cycle even in typical quantum thermodynamical settings. Novel effects such as Entanglement State Revivals, Zeno locking and thermal current interference are observed. We propose toy model devices that can be implemented harnessing the Synchronisation of a qubit (or an arbitrary collection of qubits) with a nonlinear phase oscillator. The framework theory used here, Spectral Mechanics, is a fresh look at the foundations of conventional quantum mechanics and is extensible to completely new forms of interactions and models in experimental settings.
entries.title: Quantum limit cycles from phase coupling: A framework for NISQ thermodynamic devices

entries.abstract: In sequential learning, a group of agents sequentially receives a noisy private signal and observes the predictions of prior agents to estimate a hidden ground truth. While extensively studied for binary signals, we formalize and analyze sequential learning when the hidden ground truth is an ordering of $n$ items, and both private signals and inferences involve pairwise comparisons. A key focus in sequential learning is herding, where agents disregard their private signals to follow the crowd. We show that, while local herding in our model may lead agents to make incorrect pairwise inferences, the global hidden order can still be approximated. Specifically, by aggregating all pairwise comparison outputs, the highest-ranked items can be retrieved. We investigate top-$k$ retrieval across three scenarios: (1) passive aggregation, where information is gathered from the social learning process without intervention; (2) strategic selection, where agents choose their pairwise comparisons dynamically; and (3) aggregation with stubborn nodes, where a very small set of stubborn agents, who base their inferences solely on their private signals, join the mechanism. With query complexity as the number of agents needed for a high-probability estimation, we propose top-$k$ retrieval algorithms with query complexities sublinear in $O(n^2)$, the total number of pairs.
entries.title: Social Learning of Ranking: Getting the Top Right despite Local Herding

entries.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards spends much of its rollout budget on states that yield no learning signal. We recast this as a question about the sampling distribution itself: under a fixed rollout budget, which distribution over states minimizes the variance of the policy-gradient estimator? The answer admits a closed-form Neyman allocation, $μ_{\mathrm{var}}^π(s) \propto d^π(s)\,σ_π(s)$, which connects naturally to GRPO's group-relative advantage and induces an emergent reverse curriculum as the policy improves, with no externally imposed schedule. Building on this principle, we propose VSR (Variance-driven State Resampling), a plug-in modification to GRPO using a prefix replay buffer and a zero-cost variance proxy. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks and long-horizon agentic tasks (Sokoban, BabyAI), VSR outperforms GRPO and GiGPO on most benchmarks with fewer generated tokens per update.
entries.title: Variance-Optimal State Resampling for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

entries.abstract: Workflow scheduling in user device-centric edge-cloud computing has emerged as a challenging problem due to the need to jointly optimize execution performance, energy consumption, and monetary cost. Modern workflows consist of heterogeneous tasks, where compute-intensive components are well-suited for Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) resources, while fine-grained, event-driven tasks are more efficiently executed using the Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) model. We formulate this scheduling problem for application workflows over a hybrid User Device (UD)-IaaS-FaaS computing continuum as a multi-objective Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP). The formulation models the workflow execution mechanism by incorporating cumulative capacity constraints for IaaS resources and elastic resource provisioning for FaaS. To overcome the intractability of MILP, we propose a learning-based framework that combines graph neural networks, surrogate performance modeling, and a multi-sample REINFORCE approach. The proposed approach is workflow-aware, leveraging task pairing to improve data locality and structured task placement decisions. Agent training is organized into three stages: small-scale learning of UD-IaaS trade-offs, intermediate locality aware co-location, and large-scale handling of parallelism and aggregation bottlenecks in workflows. The proposed framework is validated through real-world experiments using the Pegasus Montage workflow on a custom UD-IaaS-FaaS testbed comprising a user device, multiple IaaS nodes, and serverless FaaS instances. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the improved trade-offs across makespan, energy consumption, and cost. Compared with the genetic algorithm and greedy scheduling approaches, the proposed approach reduces makespan by 10-17.5%, energy consumption by 3-9%, and cost by 4-10%, while remaining within 3.5-5.6% of the MILP optimum.
entries.title: Learning based Scalable Multi-Objective Scheduling of Workflows across UD-IaaS-FaaS Systems

entries.abstract: False retry permission (FRP) occurs when an agent retries a timed-out tool call without support from the visible contract. RetryBench separates this error from realized recovery. Successful protected recovery does not imply reliable rejection of unsupported retries. In a 720-response key control, valid keys usually enabled safe progress, but offered changed keys elicited unsupported retries in Sol (1/80), Terra (55/80), and Luna (60/80). A later 240-response control removed the candidate and required models to supply a key. Luna still made 8/80 unsupported dispatches; Sol and Terra made none in 80 responses each. Accepting a displayed bad key therefore cannot explain all observed errors, although changed output requirements and conditions preclude a pure display-effect comparison. Removing the weak-contract label increased retries in Sol and Terra's coded-action conditions in a six-endpoint study. A separate 1,536-response canonical-action block also found a positive Terra contrast (115/128 versus 124/128 retries), concentrated in two task/order conditions; the other five contrasts remained unresolved after multiplicity correction. An explicit-contract cue control elicited deferral in all 762 returned responses, leaving recovery unresolved. These results support reporting permission and recovery together across declared interface variants. The evidence covers four purposive tasks, fixed GPT endpoints, and one recovery decision; it identifies neither internal mechanisms nor episode-level safety.
entries.title: RetryBench: Separating Retry Permission from Recovery Outcomes in GPT Tool Use

entries.abstract: Movable agents, such as autonomous vehicles and robots, should be able to autonomously adapt their pre-trained object recognition models to new environments without human annotations. While existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods address label-free model adaptation, they typically treat test data as independent snapshots, without constructively exploiting a rich, unique source of supervision: the significant variance in prediction quality as an agent observes the same object from different distances and viewpoints. To capitalize on this, we propose \texttt{MoCaFe}, a model-agnostic and hyperparameter-insensitive paradigm that leverages motion-induced prediction variance for unsupervised adaptation. Specifically, we first develop mobility-calibrated filtering of pseudo-labels, which constructs reliable pseudo-labels by fusing cross-view predictions using inverse-variance weights. The filtered pseudo-labels then guide the selection of ``hard samples'' for effective learning. To further suppress pseudo-label corruption, we introduce \texttt{p-MoCaFe}, an optional extension that uses a public dataset to assign weighting factors to data samples, yielding an estimator of the clean loss with bounded bias. Extensive experiments on autonomous driving (nuScenes, KITTI) and embodied-agent datasets show that \texttt{MoCaFe} significantly outperforms state-of-the-art TTA schemes, achieving up to approximately 20% accuracy gain.
entries.journal_ref: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
entries.title: Mobility Helps Learning: Unsupervised Model Adaptation for Object Recognition via Movement

entries.abstract: Automated failure diagnosis requires correlating browser-visible symptoms with backend observability signals, yet existing benchmarks do not evaluate this cross-modal reasoning task. Constructing one is non-trivial: multi-modal failure scenarios are costly to annotate, and live-environment capture introduces stochasticity that makes cross-run agent comparison unreliable. We present CUJBench, to our knowledge, the first benchmark to combine browser-visible failure evidence with backend observability in a diagnostic framing. CUJBench addresses annotation cost through an LLM-assisted generation pipeline with a multi-agent review loop and a three-layer annotation scheme, producing 87 labeled scenarios across five fault families, and ensures reproducibility by packaging each failure as a deterministic multi-modal snapshot with a fixed tool interface. Evaluating six LLMs under retrieval, browser-only, and full-toolset baselines, the benchmark yields an overall accuracy of 21.6% with a ceiling of 52.5%, well below saturation. Contrary to expectation, browser-only agents outperform full-toolset agents in aggregate, with expanded evidence access inducing unfocused exploration rather than improved synthesis. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-modal synthesis as the primary bottleneck: agents retrieve the decisive evidence but fail to attribute it correctly, a failure that persists across all six models and that model scale and richer tool access alone cannot resolve.
entries.title: CUJBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Browser-to-Backend Failure Diagnosis

entries.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents remains challenging in long-horizon tasks with sparse outcome rewards, where assigning credit to individual actions is difficult. Methods such as GRPO assign the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, while critic-based methods require learning an additional value function that can be costly and unstable. We introduce LLM Value Function RL (LVRL), which uses the pretrained knowledge and in-context learning ability of an LLM to estimate policy-aware state values without finetuning a separate critic. LVRL conditions the value model on group context and calibrates its predictions using known values at the initial and terminal states, enabling step-level credit assignment from estimated value differences. We further extend this idea to learning from an expert policy through on-policy distillation (OPD), introducing LLM Value Function OPD (LVOPD), which focuses teacher supervision on actions associated with decreases in estimated value. We evaluate our approach across diverse agentic benchmarks: AppWorld, BabyAI, and SWE-bench Verified. Across policy scales (4B to 32B), LVRL consistently and substantially outperforms both GRPO and PPO. On AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified, LVRL yields absolute improvements of up to 13.6 and 8.6 percentage points over GRPO. Notably, on tasks requiring extended exploration like BabyAI, LVRL bridges the gap from total failure to 75.0% success. Furthermore, LVOPD yields consistent improvements over standard distillation baselines on AppWorld. Finally, Monte-Carlo analysis confirms that our frozen critic accurately identifies semantic pitfalls and recoveries, proving that LVRL extracts robust, policy-aware step-level credit from sparse terminal outcomes.
entries.title: LLM Value Functions for Credit Assignment in Agentic RL

entries.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents are typically developed and post-trained in controlled environments with reliable tools, but deployment exposes them to tool failures, API and schema drift, and third-party services outside the developer's control. We introduce Bench2Robust, a framework for scenario-controlled solvability that augments existing benchmarks with episodes requiring retrying the original path, switching to a fallback-equivalent tool, or recognizing that no viable path remains. By controlling recoverability, Bench2Robust separates recovery-policy quality from randomness in whether failures persist or resolve. Across 7 models from 4 families and 10 task/domain slices spanning customer-service and function-calling benchmarks, 69 of 70 model-subset pairs degrade under tool failures, by up to 46.7 percentage points. We propose Bayesian Tool Memory (BTM) for structured runtime recovery context and use reinforcement learning (RL) for learned recovery behavior. On held-out Retail tasks using the benchmark's original tool set, BTM improves robustness by 16.8 percentage points without retraining, while RL retains a 6.3-point gain without inference-time BTM. Combining RL with BTM yields a 20.7-point improvement over the base model while preserving clean performance. These results show that robust tool use benefits from combining structured runtime recovery context with learned recovery behavior.
entries.title: Bench2Robust: Scenario-Controlled Recovery for Tool-Using Agents

entries.abstract: Test-Driven Development (TDD) is a widely adopted practice that requires developers to create and execute tests alongside implementation. With recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), developers can shift from manually writing the code to defining tests as executable specifications and delegating code synthesis to AI agents. However, enabling repository-level TDD under developer-written tests is challenging, requiring: (1) specification enhancement: identifying a concise yet representative test subset from large suites with rich task semantics; (2) retrieval augmentation: using tests to guide reasoning and context retrieval; and (3) test-driven refinement: interpreting test feedback for iterative improvement. We propose TENET, an agentic framework for repository-level code generation under the TDD paradigm. TENET includes: (1) a test harness mechanism that selects a concise test suite to maximize diversity of the target usage scenarios; (2) a tailored agent toolset for efficient retrieval and debugging; and (3) a reflection-based refinement workflow that iteratively analyzes failures and updates implementations. TENET consistently outperforms the strongest baselines across backbones, achieving 69.08% and 81.77% Pass@1 on RepoCod and RepoEval with Claude Sonnet 4, improving by 9.49 and 2.17 percentage points, respectively. Additionally, we present the first systematic study of how test suite characteristics influence LLM agent performance in TDD settings.
entries.comment: Accepted at the 37th IEEE International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering (ISSRE 2026)
entries.title: TENET: One Step Toward Test-Driven Development for Repository-Level Code Generation

entries.abstract: As autonomous agents are increasingly deployed, they must be able to coordinate with previously unseen agents, such as humans. This challenge has been formalized as Ad Hoc Teamwork (AHT), and has attracted a substantial body of research. However, progress has been hindered by the prohibitive computational cost of the AHT research lifecycle, lack of standardized benchmark implementations, and the absence of a diverse, validated evaluation teammate suite. This work introduces JaxAHT, the first open-source, JAX-based library designed to accelerate and standardize the AHT research lifecycle. Leveraging JAX's hardware acceleration and massive parallelization capabilities, JaxAHT provides a unified framework for teammate generation, ego agent training, and evaluation against unseen teammates, achieving approximately 95x wall-clock speedup over existing PyTorch counterparts. Along with the library, we contribute a diverse suite of evaluation teammates across Level-Based Foraging, Overcooked, and Hanabi. Using JaxAHT, we conduct a large-scale, compute-controlled benchmark study of AHT algorithms, finding that no algorithm consistently performs best, that agent modeling primarily offers benefits in role-based scenarios, and that best response returns are underestimated by reinforcement learning from scratch.
entries.title: JaxAHT: A JAX-Based Library for Ad Hoc Teamwork

entries.abstract: Inertia is intrinsic to many living and synthetic active systems, from animals and robotic agents to colloidal swimmers, and it strongly shapes transport. Many such systems employ intermittent restart protocols to regulate exploration. Stochastic resetting provides a theoretical framework for these strategies and a route to control nonequilibrium steady states, yet the role of inertia in reset-controlled active dynamics remains poorly understood. Here we study an inertial active Brownian particle in two dimensions under complete and partial stochastic resetting. We derive exact stationary second- and fourth-order scalar moments for the different protocols wherever their stationary limits exist, and obtain the full transient evolution of the mean-squared velocity and displacement under complete resetting. Under complete resetting, inertia strongly enhances localization: at large reset rates, the steady-state mean-squared displacement decays as $r^{-3}$, rather than following the overdamped scaling $r^{-1}$. Kurtosis-based phase diagrams reveal strongly non-Gaussian position and velocity statistics, including activity-induced re-entrant behavior as a function of reset rate and inertia. The transient solutions show that resetting shifts the velocity-relaxation rates, whereas the terminal relaxation of the displacement is governed solely by the mean resetting time $1/r$, with inertia controlling the faster transient modes. Comparing complete resetting with the partial protocols, we find that resetting the velocity together with the position substantially enhances localization. Resetting the orientation to a fixed or a random direction drives the mean-squared velocity toward opposite limits. These results establish inertia, reset frequency, and the choice of reset variables as coupled control parameters for localization, relaxation, and non-Gaussian fluctuations in active systems.
entries.title: Controlling inertial active Brownian motion via stochastic resetting

entries.abstract: Existing multi-turn image editing paradigms are often confined to isolated single-step execution. Due to a lack of context-awareness and closed-loop feedback mechanisms, they are prone to error accumulation and semantic drift during multi-turn interactions, ultimately resulting in severe structural distortion of the generated images. To address this, we propose IMAGAgent, a multi-turn image editing agent framework based on a ``plan--execute--reflect'' closed-loop mechanism that achieves deep synergy among instruction parsing, tool scheduling, and adaptive correction within a unified pipeline. Specifically, we first present a constraint-aware planning module that leverages a vision-language model (VLM) to precisely decompose complex natural language instructions into a series of executable sub-tasks, governed by target singularity, semantic atomicity, and visual perceptibility. Then, the tool-chain orchestration module dynamically constructs execution paths based on the current image, the current sub-task, and the historical context, enabling adaptive scheduling and collaborative operation among heterogeneous operation models covering image retrieval, segmentation, detection, and editing. Finally, we devise a multi-expert collaborative reflection mechanism in which a central large language model (LLM) synthesizes evaluations from multiple vision-language models into holistic feedback, triggering fine-grained self-correction and recording feedback outcomes to optimize future decisions. Extensive experiments on our constructed MTEditBench and the MagicBrush dataset demonstrate that IMAGAgent achieves performance significantly superior to existing methods in terms of instruction consistency, editing precision, and overall quality. The code is available at https://github.com/hackermmzz/IMAGAgent.
entries.title: IMAGAgent: Orchestrating Multi-Turn Image Editing via Constraint-Aware Planning and Reflection

entries.abstract: Swarms of LLM-assisted autonomous robots are increasingly proposed for cooperative intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) in contested environments. A growing class of their assurance failures arises not within any single platform but across the swarm: individually-compliant actions compose into a mission-level violation: a prohibited objective split across platforms to evade per-platform limits, or a collective budget quietly exceeded. Per-platform guardrails miss these by construction, and contested communications let the violation hide behind lost or delayed evidence. We present a three-tier (platform/squad/mission) compositional runtime-verification framework that decomposes a mission policy into per-agent and cross-agent aspects, aggregates per-platform verdicts over a verification-aware messaging fabric, and fuses them with an evidence-aware, two-axis (security x completeness) algebra whose provenance names the platforms that jointly triggered a violation. Because the fabric makes evidence loss and silence observable, unsupported negative verdicts are downgraded to an explicit unknown rather than reported as mission-wide all-clears. On a simulated ISR mission, an indirect prompt injection that causes real LLM planners to split a prohibited collection task across four platforms is invisible to every per-platform monitor yet detected compositionally with full provenance; under an injected fault campaign a best-effort central monitor emits silent false all-clears while the verification-aware fabric emits none.
entries.title: Mission-Level Runtime Assurance for LLM-Assisted ISR Swarms over a Verification-Aware Fabric

entries.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as teams, yet they fail in characteristically social ways: information holders stay silent, dominant speakers anchor groups on wrong answers, and norm violations go unsanctioned. We present Agent Sociodrama, a framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agent teams. Under fixed personas, agents' emotional states and directed, asymmetric relationships are updated every round by a unified external LLM judge and shape their subsequent interactions. Across six LLM backbones and five social scenarios, we assess social fidelity through classical social-theory patterns and agreement with human judgments. The resulting trajectories exhibit structured social patterns and model-specific differences. We then introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting (TPR), which diagnoses group-dynamic failures from interaction transcripts and social trajectories and recasts agent personas before rerunning the task. Across four collaborative benchmarks, TPR improves performance from both heterogeneous and randomly initialized agent persona compositions, yielding up to 83.3%p of accuracy improvement over the initial casting. On representative distributed-information cooperation and mixed-motive bargaining tasks, we outperform SOTOPIA and AgentVerse in three of four comparisons, by up to 37.5%p in Pareto rate. These results show that validated social trajectories provide actionable signals for repairing LLM agent teams.
entries.title: Agent Sociodrama: Social-Dynamics-Guided Persona Recasting for LLM Agent Teams

entries.abstract: A principal funds an agent's project over two periods, with a midterm review providing a public signal about project quality. The agent privately knows the project's quality and always prefers more funding, while the principal wants to match funding to quality. A natural benchmark uses the review only after it arrives, to update beliefs and improve the second-period allocation. The optimal mechanism instead frontloads the review's information value: it also uses the review as an incentive device to elicit truthful reporting up front, thereby strictly improving the principal's first-period expected payoff. In the optimal mechanism, higher-quality projects receive more funding initially but face larger cuts after a bad review, leaving them with less funding than lower-quality projects. A good review increases funding, but the resulting allocation need not preserve the initial ranking of projects and eventually declines with quality.
entries.title: Resource Allocation with Midterm Review

entries.abstract: Precision medical robotics demands adaptive decision-making under strict safety, interpretability, and execution constraints. Although recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models show strong multimodal reasoning ability, their continuous action generation paradigm is not well suited for precision medical tasks, where reliable closed-loop operation may also depend on non-action system function calls. To address this gap, we propose MedVLA, a hierarchical framework that couples high-level multimodal reasoning with low-level function-constrained execution. We further introduce a scalable multi-agent pipeline to generate skill-oriented chain-of-thought(CoT) data for structured training. Built on different multimodal large-model backbones, MedVLA consistently improves performance after fine-tuning, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework across model variants. Under identical initial conditions, we perform 100 closed-loop flexible electrode implantation trials. The results show that MedVLA achieves a 95.0\% task success rate, substantially outperforming representative VLA baselines, including OpenVLA (8\%) and $π_0$ (15\%), in accuracy, stability, and safety. These results indicate that structured reasoning with constrained function-level execution is a practical route toward deployable precision medical robotics.
entries.title: MedVLA: A Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Framework for Closed-Loop Precision Medical Robot Manipulation

entries.abstract: Vision-language navigation requires agents to follow natural-language instructions to reach target locations, making high-quality language supervision essential. Since human annotation is costly, prior work has explored scalable data synthesis methods. However, existing methods typically either use separate models for navigation and instruction generation or couple the two tasks through task-specific components; most also annotate the full trajectory corpus with a fixed model before updating, which can cause generated supervision to lag behind the evolving policy. Therefore, we introduce RSI-Nav, a data-centric recursive self-improvement framework for navigation via policy-synchronized language-action dual bootstrapping, which unifies vision-language-to-action instruction following and vision-action-to-language instruction generation within a shared model. Specifically, after supervised fine-tuning establishes fundamental capabilities, RSI-Nav progressively processes unlabeled trajectories in small shards. The current model generates instructions for these trajectories, executes them to evaluate goal completion and path efficiency, retains qualified samples, and immediately updates itself before processing the next shard. This shard-wise update keeps newly generated supervision aligned with the evolving policy. We also incorporate spatial understanding data, since stronger spatial reasoning benefits navigation. Extensive experiments show that RSI-Nav reaches 68.6% SR on R2R-CE and 72.4% SR on RxR-CE, while providing stronger instruction-generation utility and modestly improved spatial understanding after recursive evolution.
entries.title: Data-Centric Recursive Self-Improvement for Navigation via Policy-Synchronized Language-Action Dual Bootstrapping

entries.abstract: Recent focus in agentic reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to improve credit assignment in long-horizon tasks. One promising direction combines reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), integrating trajectory-level advantages with dense token-level supervision. This line of work often conditions a teacher model on privileged context, such as agentic skills, to score tokens generated by the student policy. Despite their progress, they largely overlook the on-policy evolution of agentic skills and the reliability of teacher supervision. Towards this end, we introduce Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization (RSIPO), a self-evolving agentic RL framework that enables agentic skills and the policy model to co-evolve throughout the training process. Specifically, RSIPO enables the policy itself to extract skills from completed trajectories and explicitly optimizes its skill-generation capability through trajectory replay. It further employs empirical Bayes shrinkage to dynamically calibrate the student's trust in teacher scores, accounting for the fact that skill-enhanced teacher guidance can sometimes be less reliable. Experiments with Qwen-family models on embodied interaction and search-based agentic tasks demonstrate that RSIPO outperforms all the compared baseline approaches. With Qwen2.5-7B as the base model, RSIPO achieves an average success rate of 98.6\% on ALFWorld, yielding absolute improvements of 2.5\% and 17.4\% over the second-best baseline and standard GRPO, respectively.
entries.title: RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution

entries.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and vision--language--action models have provided robots with new capabilities for long-horizon task understanding and planning. In surgical robotics, however, end-to-end prediction of low-level actions remains limited by insufficient precision, opaque decisions, and scarce data. This paper presents SurgiCLAW, a hierarchical skill-based framework for precision surgical manipulation. SurgiCLAW confines an MLLM to intraoperative visual understanding, structured explanation, and atomic surgical-skill selection, while delegating physical execution to verifiable deterministic control programs. For brain--machine-interface implantation, a representative high-precision surgical task, we construct a state-to-skill invocation dataset and expand it through visual and state perturbations. The model first learns structured skill invocation through supervised fine-tuning and is then optimized using three rewards for action correctness, operation prerequisites, and format validity, improving action selection, operational safety, and output parseability. We evaluate subtask success, offline model comparison, real-robot performance, and ablations. On a fixed test set, SurgiCLAW achieves 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1). Across 50 closed-loop real-robot implantation trials, it achieves an 88.0% task success rate.
entries.title: SurgiCLAW: An Interpretable Atomic-Skill Agent for Precision Robotic Micromanipulation

entries.abstract: Geospatial agents are increasingly expected to support recurring and evolving analytical tasks rather than execute isolated workflows. In such settings, effective agents must distill prior execution experience into reusable geospatial procedural knowledge to guide future planning and tool use. However, existing memory-augmented paradigms struggle to summarize both long-horizon tool-chain orchestration experience and tool-level invocation constraints in geospatial analysis, while directly relying on LLM self-reflection to update experience often leads to misattribution and unreliable revisions. To address these challenges, we propose GeoSkill, an experience-driven hierarchical skill learning framework for geospatial agents. GeoSkill comprises two core components: (i) a Hierarchical Skill Bank (HSB), consisting of a Planning Skill Bank and a Tool Skill Bank, which respectively distill high-level task-planning experience and tool usage constraints, enabling structured representation and cross-task reuse of historical execution experience; and (ii) a Collaborative Trace-driven Skill Revision (CTSR) mechanism, where Judge, Critic, and Refiner collaboratively perform error identification, skill-level defect localization, and targeted modification, preventing misattributed and unreliable revisions from polluting the skill bank. GeoSkill learns and validates skills from historical executions during development, and freezes the skill bank for retrieval-only guidance on unseen tasks during deployment. Extensive experiments on EarthBench and ThinkGeo demonstrate that GeoSkill effectively transforms historical execution experience into reusable hierarchical skills, improving both end-to-end task accuracy and tool-execution reliability in geospatial tasks.
entries.comment: Withdraw the submission, citing numerical errors
entries.title: GeoSkill:Experience-Driven Hierarchical Skill Learning with Collaborative Revision forGeospatialAgents

entries.abstract: Large language model agents are emerging as an important new class of users of desktop applications. However, existing desktop interfaces were designed for human end users or application developers, leaving agents to interpret visual controls or discover and compose low-level software operations. This mismatch can hinder even capable agents, yet it remains unclear what interface properties make desktop software easier for agents to use. To study this question, we treat software evolution as a natural source of interface variation and introduce DeskIF-Bench, a benchmark of 255 artifact-verified tasks across six desktop applications. By holding the task, agent, and verifier fixed while varying the software release, we measure how interface changes affect agent performance. Across two models and six applications, the newest release consistently outperforms the oldest. Trajectory analysis identifies three relevant interface properties: discoverability, granularity, and observability. Guided by these properties, we develop ANIS, a framework that synthesizes agent-native interfaces from the capabilities of installed applications. On an expanded evaluation of 368 tasks across eight applications, atomic interfaces improve success over native SDK use by 3.8 and 3.5 percentage points with DeepSeek V4 Flash and Claude Haiku 4.5, respectively, while reducing online token usage by approximately 73%. Goal-level commands further raise success to 74.5% and 67.4%, respectively.
entries.title: A Decade in a Day: Synthesizing Agent-Native Interfaces from Human-Oriented Software Evolution

entries.abstract: Google Earth AI is a family of geospatial AI models, together with an agent that orchestrates them. We present this agent, Google Earth AI's Geospatial Reasoning agent (GRA), a Gemini-powered research system that combines geospatial data sources, foundation models, and tools to answer questions about our planet. GRA organizes these into modular domain skills and pairs them with upfront geospatial planning to decompose complex queries into multi-stage workflows. Evaluating such systems is hard: real-world problems admit multiple valid workflows, require data discovery across large catalogs, and rely on evolving ground truth. We introduce two benchmarks and release their development splits. GeoExpertQueries poses complex analytical problems grounded in practitioner use cases and refined by geospatial experts; each is paired with a consensus golden workflow from three independent experts and scored by a human-validated, tool-agnostic autorater. GeoKTools consists of templated queries with deterministic reference solvers that systematically vary the number of required tool types. We also use two external benchmarks, CBGB and UnivEARTH; the latter we find to be saturated. To isolate the contribution of GRA's tools and its agentic orchestration, we compare four configurations, each with Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3.8 Flash: a standalone LLM, the LLM with basic tools, the LLM with GRA's skills and tools but without its upfront planning and execution guidance, and GRA itself. With at most basic tools, an advanced model recovers much of the answer on templated queries but satisfies only a small fraction of the expert workflows on open-ended problems; GRA performs well on both. The largest step comes from GRA's skills and tools; on open-ended problems, its planning and execution guidance add a further gain with Gemini 3.8 Flash, letting Flash match or exceed Pro at lower cost.
entries.comment: 39 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables (10 main tables, 1 appendix table)
entries.title: Google Earth AI Geospatial Reasoning Agent: Capabilities and a Systematic Evaluation

entries.abstract: Scene classification of remote sensing imagery with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is formulated as a single-forward-pass decision problem: candidate class names are lettered options in the prompt, a registered answer slot is conditioned on the prompt, and classification is read out by scoring letter tokens with the language-modeling head. We show that although this letter binding is highly effective within its training vocabulary (97.71% OA on UCM), it behaves erratically out of vocabulary: zero-adaptation accuracy across four cross-dataset directions fluctuates between 7.35% and 96.40%, and under out-of-vocabulary weights its confidence fails inversely on open-set evaluation, assigning higher confidence to unseen than to seen classes (AUROC 0.38), a failure we term silent hallucination. We retain the slot representation and replace the readout with RSAJEV, a training-free abstaining prototype memory that performs retrieval-based prototype matching: K reference images per class are cached as prototypes via their slot representations under the same prompt, and classification becomes nearest-neighbor retrieval over the prototypes, refined by a shrinkage-Mahalanobis geometric correction. This readout is mechanistically isomorphic to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) but operates on discriminative decisions; it is the first retrieval-based readout for MLLM slot representations. The retrieval readout reaches 89.43% on the UCM cross-dataset gate with 16 references per class and zero gradient updates, and 96.90% on AID. Its ID-ness scores attain 0.91-0.99 AUROC on open-set evaluation over two datasets, exceeding symbolic confidence (0.38-0.96) in all four open-set settings, restoring a calibratable abstention channel and supporting class addition/removal at zero extra inference cost via offline rescoring of the cached matrix.
entries.title: RSAJEV: Training-Free Abstaining Prototype Memory for Eliminating Silent Hallucination in JEV-Based Remote Sensing Classification

entries.abstract: LLM optimization loops often show the proposer the candidates it has already tried and rejected, but leave it to the proposer to avoid them. We ask whether avoidance measured in a static probe predicts avoidance in the states an optimizer's own trajectory produces. In catalog-based loops where three open LLMs improve a GUI agent by naming one of 40 edits, a re-proposal is identified exactly by the edit's name. Clean base-state probes underpredict re-proposal in the proposers' own loops (macro-averaged loop-minus-probe rate 0.32 [0.27, 0.37]), and proposals of already evaluated harness-edit pairs consume 28-63% of valid proposer iterations. The two settings reject different edits: a probe's rejected edits are mostly ones the proposer did not choose, whereas a loop's are its own earlier choices, which remain preferred when the history is removed. Ordinary history lowers re-proposal for two proposers but raises it for the third, and the effects of failure evidence are model-specific. Stating the rejection status in one sentence lowers re-proposal in every model (-0.16 [-0.22, -0.09] relative to a neutral list of the same IDs). For catalog-based loops with exact edit identities, rejection avoidance should be measured on the rejected sets the loop produces.
entries.title: Visible but Not Avoided: State-Dependent Re-Proposal of Rejected Candidates in Catalog-Based LLM Optimization Loops

entries.abstract: Healthcare agents must transform longitudinal clinical evidence into reliable actions through heterogeneous tools and stateful workflows, conditions under which model-centric systems may lose context, misuse tools, fail to verify consequential transitions, or cross authorization boundaries. Existing medical-agent benchmarks primarily emphasize terminal task outcomes, making it difficult to determine whether execution failures arise from the agent model, the runtime harness, or their interaction. We present the Medical Harness Protocol, an outcome-preserving framework that independently evaluates seven healthcare-specific process dimensions: Care Action Fulfillment, Clinical Resource Competence, Patient-Evidence Alignment, Clinical Workflow Continuity, Clinical Auditability, Closed-Loop Verification, and Clinical Conduct Boundaries. A normalized intervention trace further tracks whether runtime support is available, activated, delivered, adopted by the agent, and propagated into subsequent behavior. We instantiate the protocol as MedHarnessBench, comprising 342 executable tasks across FHIR/EHR operations, healthcare-administration interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools. Across more than 16,000 controlled task executions, MedHarness yields broad improvements in terminal task success, intermediate subtask completion, and healthcare-specific process quality. We further evaluate MedHarness against multiple general-purpose harnesses and use controlled single-fault perturbations to verify the sensitivity and discrimination of the seven-dimensional evaluation. These results demonstrate that healthcare-specific runtime support can substantially improve both task completion and execution quality, while revealing failures that terminal outcomes alone cannot capture. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Tomry1114/Awesome-Agent-Harness-for-Healthcare.
entries.title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation

entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong abilities in writing and revising programs, yet many program-synthesis benchmarks still evaluate programs in symbolic or digital environments. We introduce compositional machine design, a physically grounded form of program synthesis where machines are written as programs that compose standardized parts, and success is determined by simulated physical behavior. To study this problem, we present BesiegeField, a testbed built on the machine-building game Besiege. In BesiegeField, LLM agents generate machine programs from textual functional demands, execute the resulting machines in simulation, and receive rewards and state feedback. We benchmark LLM agents across representative machine-design tasks under single-agent generation, iterative editing, and hierarchical workflows. Strong models recover task-relevant structures and sometimes achieve nontrivial physical performance, but often struggle with spatially precise assembly, mechanism-level planning, and translating feedback into useful structural edits. We further finetune Qwen2.5-14B, an open-source LLM, with reinforcement learning from simulation-derived rewards. We find that, under a fixed generation budget, RL improves the best machine discovered. We additionally evaluate human performance to provide a reference point for task difficulty. These results establish compositional machine design as a testbed for studying LLM agents that synthesize executable machine programs and improve them through physical feedback.
entries.comment: 75 pages, 44 figures, Project Page: https://besiegefield.github.io, accepted at EMNLP 2026 Main Conference (Oral)
entries.title: Compositional Machine Design as Program Synthesis with LLMs

entries.abstract: Coding agents based on frozen language models can improve their performance by refining the external context they rely on, without updating model weights. We study recursive self-improvement through behavioral specifications: natural-language code documentation that describes the behavior of program entities and guides agents in generating correct code. We formulate a self-improvement loop in which an agent generates code from its current specifications, evaluates it with execution-verified tests, and refines the specifications based on observed failures. The improved specifications then guide subsequent generation, progressively improving the agent's understanding of the codebase. However, recursive refinement is challenging because program entities are interdependent. Improving the specification of one entity can inadvertently degrade the correctness of others, a phenomenon we call output coupling. This creates a whack-a-mole effect in which local improvements cause regressions elsewhere, preventing consistent progress. We introduce SpecForge, a multi-frontier tree search framework that addresses this challenge with three mechanisms: (i) Pareto-guided state selection preserves complementary specification states and prevents premature commitment; (ii) dependency-constrained entity selection prioritizes callee-before-caller refinement; and (iii) error-diversified expansion explores multiple refinements using different subsets of test failures. On DevEval+, SpecForge achieves the best performance across five backbone models, including a 94.9% solve rate with Claude-4.5-Sonnet and a 5.7-percentage-point average improvement over the strongest baseline. The improved specifications also make the agent better at tasks outside the loop: they transfer to cross-language translation and to new-feature implementation, where they outperform the benchmark-provided requirement documents.
entries.title: SpecForge: Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents via Behavioral Specifications

entries.abstract: Can AI make Software Engineering (SE) -- the discipline -- obsolete? And can it make software engineers -- the professionals -- redundant? This paper argues that the rise of capable AI coding agents makes SE and software engineers essential, not obsolete: the missing foundation without which AI-assisted development produces misleadingly plausible, unverifiable, and ultimately untrustworthy software. Three structural properties of large language models (probabilistic generation, agnosticism, and semantic statelessness) create a structural vacuum that no amount of training can eliminate. Filling it requires four knowledge levers: methodological knowledge, domain knowledge, design choices, and process choices. All four must be reified as persistent artifacts, and each requires the software engineer as methodologist, mediator, and custodian.
entries.comment: Accepted for publication in Communications of the ACM. 6 pages. v2: final version submitted to the publisher; Section 1 updated with evidence published since July 2026
entries.title: Why Software Engineering Is Indispensable in the Age of Coding Agents

entries.abstract: Scaling on-policy distillation (OPD) for large language models (LLMs) confronts a fundamental tension: asynchronous execution is necessary for system efficiency, but structurally deviates from the ideal on-policy objective. To address this challenge, we theoretically decompose the objective discrepancy into rollout drift and supervision drift, capturing staleness in student rollout and teacher context, respectively. Building on this, we introduce a sample-level freshness score that quantifies the reliability of a buffered sample with respect to the on-policy objective. Guided by this signal, we further propose f-OPD, a novel framework that adaptively regulates stale-sample influence and constrains policy drift accumulated under asynchronous training. Across reasoning, tool-use, and coding-agent tasks of increasing interaction horizon, f-OPD consistently achieves task performance comparable to synchronous optimization while largely retaining the throughput advantages of asynchronous execution.
